title: Robust Table Detection and Structure Recognition from Heterogeneous Document Images
research_question: Can a unified visual pipeline robustly detect tables and recover their row, column, and spanning-cell structure across heterogeneous, distorted, curved, and sparsely ruled document images?
methodology: RobusTabNet first detects table regions using a CornerNet-style proposal mechanism that predicts opposing corners and exhaustively groups them, followed by Fast R-CNN classification and box refinement. Its table-structure recognizer uses a split-and-merge strategy: spatial CNN modules predict long-range row and column separator masks, geometric post-processing converts those masks into a cell grid, and a Grid CNN decides which adjacent grid cells should be merged into spanning cells. The models use lightweight ResNet-18/FPN components and are evaluated on public table-detection and structure datasets including cTDaR, PubLayNet, IIIT-AR-13K, SciTSR, and PubTabNet, as well as an in-house dataset containing challenging distorted and curved tables. Evaluation reports detection AP, precision, recall, F1, weighted-average F1, and TEDS-Struct, together with component ablations.

key_findings.finding: The CornerNet-plus-Fast-R-CNN detector achieves a weighted-average F1 of 94.9% on cTDaR TrackA, exceeding the comparison methods reported in the table.
On PubLayNet, the ResNet-18 detector reports AP 97.0 over IoU 0.5:0.95 and AP 92.0 at IoU 0.95, indicating particularly accurate localization at strict overlap thresholds.
The structure recognizer reports F1 99.3% on SciTSR and 98.7% on the more complicated SciTSR-COMP subset.
On PubTabNet, the method reports a TEDS-Struct score of 97.0%, above the listed comparison systems.
On the authors' distorted and curved in-house data, weighted-average F1 rises from 63.8% for SPLERGE to 94.6% for the proposed recognizer.
The Grid CNN cell-merging component raises weighted-average F1 from 90.9% without merging to 94.6%, and exceeds the tested relation-network and GCN alternatives.
The system recognizes geometry and cell structure within individual images but provides no mechanism for associating a detected table or cell with its counterpart in a later revision.

limitations: Nearby tables can be difficult to separate reliably.
Multi-line cell content can make separation-line estimation difficult.
Extremely dense tables can fail when masks for adjacent separation lines overlap.
The authors note that available datasets are dominated by black text on white backgrounds, leaving generalization to different backgrounds, fonts, and line colors insufficiently tested.
The challenging distorted-table evaluation uses an in-house dataset whose public availability is not established in the paper.
The method extracts table structure but does not assign durable cross-version table, row, column, or cell identifiers.
No document-revision provenance model or message-to-table reference-resolution mechanism is included.
raw_claims: RobusTabNet separates table processing into table detection and table structure recognition.
The detector generates table proposals from predicted corner pairs and then uses Fast R-CNN to reject or refine proposals.
The structure-recognition stage first splits a table into a grid and then merges grid cells when they belong to the same logical cell.
Spatial CNN propagation is used to capture long-range evidence for row and column separators.
Grid CNN performs visual reasoning over neighboring cells to recover spanning-cell structure.
The method is evaluated on several public benchmarks for both table detection and table structure recognition.
The reported SciTSR F1 is 99.3%, while the complicated subset score is 98.7%.
The reported PubTabNet TEDS-Struct score is 97.0%.
Experiments on an in-house dataset show a large advantage over SPLERGE for distorted and curved tables.
The authors identify very dense tables as a remaining failure mode because separator masks can overlap.
The system does not address longitudinal matching of cells or regions after a document is revised.
